source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Weeds do not only compete with corn for soil fertility — they also compete for sunlight, air, and water. When rainfall is insufficient, especially during the early wet-season planting window, poor weed control seriously reduces yield through this competition for nutrients, light, air, and above all water. The overall goal of weed management is to keep the weed population as low as possible from the start, and to continue reducing it further as the season goes on — this is a key element of successful weed control.

A central question in pre-plant weed management is timing: when should a field be ploughed relative to weed germination? Generally, weeds begin germinating about 4-5 days after rain falls and soil gains moisture, and will continue emerging afterward. It is recommended to plough the field only after weeds have had time to germinate, and then turn them under — rather than ploughing before weeds emerge. If a field is ploughed before weeds emerge with the intent of suppressing their growth, this does not work as intended; instead it can loosen the soil and expose weed seeds/roots, resulting in even more weed growth. To reduce weed growth effectively, the recommended practice is to plough roughly 10 days after rainfall.

Herbicide use before ploughing: when there are many weeds already germinated, it is better to apply herbicide before final ploughing, to ensure weeds are killed before the field is turned over. In Cambodia, two herbicide types are commonly used at this pre-plant stage: a systemic, non-selective type (glyphosate, locally referred to in the Pailin area as "ទឹកខ្មៅ"/Teuk Khmao) and a contact, non-selective type (referred to in the source as "ដោខ្វត", locally called "ទឹកសៀវ" in Pailin, sold under a brand whose label shows the active ingredient paraquat dichloride) — see the separate herbicide entries in this dataset for full details on each product.
